stops.title: The Plague of Justinian
stops.blurb: In 541 a deadly epidemic broke out in the Eastern Roman Empire, in the reign of the emperor Justinian. Outbreaks kept returning for two centuries, until about 750. DNA from graves in Britain, France, Spain, Germany and Austria shows the disease was plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, the same germ behind the later Black Death. How many people it killed is still argued over.
stops.debate: Older estimates put the deaths in the tens of millions. Mordechai and colleagues argue that coins, laws, papyri, pollen and graves show no sign of a collapse on that scale.

stops.title: Islam and the caliphates
stops.blurb: In the early 600s Muhammad, a man of Mecca in Arabia, began preaching a new faith, Islam, based on revelations Muslims believe he received from God. In 622 he and his followers moved to Medina, the year the Muslim calendar counts from. Within eighty years of his death in 632, the caliphs, his successors as leaders of the community, ruled from Persia to Spain.

stops.title: Maya kingdoms break up; Cahokia rises and falls
stops.blurb: In the Maya lowlands of Mexico and Central America, wet centuries helped kingdoms multiply. A drying trend from about 660 brought more warfare, and the kingdoms broke up one by one; a long drought from 1020 to 1100 followed. Far to the north, by the Mississippi, Cahokia became the largest town in what is now the United States, until floods and droughts around 1150 put it under strain.
stops.debate: Kennett and colleagues tie the Maya breakup to drought, a view still contested. At Cahokia, climate is one of several proposed causes of decline, alongside environmental damage and political change.

stops.title: Baghdad's House of Wisdom, and algebra
stops.blurb: The Abbasid caliphs founded a new capital, Baghdad, in 762. Under the caliph al-Mamun, who ruled from 813, scholars at its House of Wisdom translated Greek science and philosophy into Arabic and built observatories. One of them, al-Khwarizmi, wrote the book whose title gave us the word algebra, and another explaining the Indian way of writing numbers with nine digits and zero.
stops.dateNote: Al-Khwarizmi lived from about 780 to about 850; exact dates for his books are not known.

stops.title: Printing, paper money, gunpowder and the compass
stops.blurb: In 868 a Buddhist scripture, the Diamond Sutra, was printed in China from carved wooden blocks; it is the oldest printed book that carries a date. Under the Song dynasty (960 to 1279) came movable type made of clay, the first government paper money in the 1020s, a written gunpowder recipe in 1044, and the first description of a magnetic compass, in 1088.

stops.title: The Swahili coast and Great Zimbabwe
stops.blurb: The Swahili towns of the East African coast traded across eastern Africa and the Indian Ocean, and their people were among the first south of the Sahara to practise Islam. Ancient DNA shows African and Persian ancestry mixing there from about 1000. Inland, the stone-walled town of Great Zimbabwe held Chinese porcelain, Islamic glass and glass beads brought by long-distance trade.
stops.debate: Great Zimbabwe is often said to have held 18,000 to 20,000 people. Chirikure and colleagues estimate a few thousand at any one time.

stops.title: The Norse in Newfoundland
stops.blurb: Around the year 1000, Norse sailors from Greenland built a small camp at L'Anse aux Meadows, on the northern tip of Newfoundland. Wood they cut there with metal tools comes from trees felled in 1021, a date fixed by a burst of cosmic rays in 993 that left a mark in tree rings. They stayed only a few years. It is the oldest known European site in the Americas.
stops.dateNote: 1021 is the year the cut trees were felled. The Norse presence may have begun a few years earlier.

stops.title: Chola, Srivijaya and Angkor
stops.blurb: Kingdoms around the Bay of Bengal grew rich on sea trade between India and China. Chinese records describe Srivijaya, on Sumatra, forcing passing ships to call at its ports. In 1025 the Chola king Rajendra of south India sent a fleet that raided them. Inland, the Khmer capital of Angkor, home of Angkor Wat, grew into the largest settlement complex of the preindustrial world.
stops.debate: Why Rajendra sent the fleet is not recorded. Historians have proposed a trade war, plunder, or conquest for its own sake.

stops.title: Polynesian voyagers settle the last islands
stops.blurb: Across an ocean covering a third of the Earth, Polynesian voyagers settled the last large habitable lands. Radiocarbon dates suggest people reached the Society Islands around 1025 to 1120, then spread in one burst to Hawaii, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and Aotearoa (New Zealand) between about 1190 and 1290. Their genes show they also met people from South America around 1200.
stops.debate: Older studies put the first settlement centuries earlier. Wilmshurst and colleagues argue those dates came from unreliable samples; genetic studies give a broadly similar sequence.

stops.title: The Mongol Empire
stops.blurb: In 1206 an assembly of Mongol nobles gave the leader Temujin the title Chinggis Khan. He and his successors conquered the largest contiguous land empire in history. By 1300 it had split into four khanates, from China to Persia and the Russian steppe. Under this Mongol peace, merchants, missionaries and envoys crossed Eurasia more easily than before.
stops.debate: Why the Mongols expanded is not agreed. Tree rings show fifteen unusually wet years as Chinggis rose, which fed grass and horses; other accounts stress a cold spell that stressed pastures, and broken trade with China.

stops.title: Mansa Musa and the gold of Mali
stops.blurb: For some 800 years, from the 700s to the 1500s, camel caravans carried West African gold across the Sahara. In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of Mali, passed through Cairo on pilgrimage to Mecca. The scholar al-Umari wrote that he gave away so much gold that its price in Egypt fell for years. Back home, Timbuktu grew into a centre of Islamic learning.

stops.title: Tenochtitlan and the Inca
stops.blurb: Around 1325 the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, in the Valley of Mexico. They added farmland on raised beds called chinampas, and causeways that doubled as dikes, until the city covered more than 13 square kilometres. In the Andes, the Inca of Cusco began a rapid expansion in the 1400s; their estate at Machu Picchu was in use by about 1420.
stops.debate: Spanish-era accounts date the start of Inca expansion to the ruler Pachacuti in 1438. Radiocarbon dates from Machu Picchu suggest it began about two decades earlier.

stops.title: The Black Death
stops.blurb: Between 1346 and 1353, plague swept around the Black Sea and the Mediterranean and into the lands beyond. DNA from graves near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan, where tombstones dated 1338 and 1339 name pestilence as the cause of death, points to a source in Central Asia. In the worst-hit places perhaps half the people died, while some regions escaped lightly.
stops.debate: The often-quoted figure of half the population is uncertain. Pollen records show farming collapsing in some regions and carrying on almost unchanged in others.

stops.title: Zheng He's fleets
stops.blurb: Between 1405 and 1433, the Ming court sent seven great fleets into the Indian Ocean under the admiral Zheng He. The first carried nearly 28,000 men in 317 ships. They called at Malacca, Calicut, Hormuz, Aden and the East African coast, bringing envoys back to China. Then officials at court turned against the cost, and the voyages stopped.

p: By the late 600s, during the Tang dynasty, Buddhist texts were being printed in China from wooden blocks. A whole page of text and pictures was carved in reverse into one block, inked, and pressed onto paper. The practice reached Korea and Japan by about 800. The oldest surviving printed book with a date is a copy of the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist scripture. Its last lines say a man named Wang Jie had it made in 868 for free distribution, on behalf of his parents.

Under the Song dynasty (960 to 1279) the pace of invention quickened. An artisan named Bi Sheng, who died in 1051, made movable type: one small piece of baked clay for each character, which could be set in a frame, printed and reused. Merchants had long traded paper receipts for coins left with deposit shops; in the 1020s the government took over and issued the first state paper money. A military manual of 1044 gives the first true recipe for gunpowder. The scholar Shen Kuo, writing around 1088, gave the first description of a magnetic needle compass, and noted that it does not point exactly north.

The Diamond Sutra survived because it was sealed in a cave at Dunhuang, on the Silk Roads in northwest China, some time before about 1000. A monk found the hidden library around 1900, and the scroll is now in the British Library. Bi Sheng's clay type is described in Shen Kuo's book. The gunpowder recipe comes from the 1044 manual itself. No Song paper notes survive; the oldest paper money we can hold is a Ming note of 1375.

The dates of some firsts depend on how they are defined. The compass is a good example: Shen Kuo described the magnetic needle around 1088, but Columbia University's account places the first reports of the compass being used in a new way, with a smaller needle fixed on a stem and sometimes cased for sea travel, in 1119. Movable type is another. In China it was never widely used, because carving whole blocks was cheaper. Korea was casting metal type by the 1230s, and a Buddhist book printed there with metal type in 1377, known as the Jikji, survives in Paris. Whether Johannes Gutenberg, who printed his Bible around 1455, drew on any Asian example is not known.

Cheap printed books helped literacy spread and fed popular reading and drama in Song cities. Paper money made large trade easier. Gunpowder changed warfare: Song engineers built fire lances, bombs, rockets and early cannons, and the Mongols and other neighbours soon took up the same weapons. Each of these began in China and later reshaped life far beyond it.

Norse sailors, the seafaring people of Scandinavia often called Vikings, had made homes in Iceland and Greenland. Around the year 1000 some of them sailed further west and reached North America. At L'Anse aux Meadows, on the northern tip of Newfoundland, they built eight buildings with sod walls and roofs over wooden frames, like houses in Iceland and Greenland at the time. They had workshops and a small forge where they smelted iron, the first time iron was smelted in the Americas. Then they left, probably after only a few years, and the buildings decayed.

The Norse stories called sagas, first written down in the 1100s and 1200s, tell of voyages from Greenland to a land called Vinland. In one, the Greenlander Leif Eriksson sets up a camp there; in another, a later expedition fights with the local people, whom the Norse called skrælings, and goes home because it is badly outnumbered. For a long time nobody knew whether these stories described real places.

In 1960 the Norwegian explorer Helge Ingstad, guided by a local man, George Decker, found low grassy ridges at L'Anse aux Meadows. He and the archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad led excavations there for eight years. Iron slag and iron boat rivets showed the site was Norse, because the Indigenous peoples of the area did not work iron then. A spindle whorl and a needle fragment, tools often linked with women's work, suggest that some of the settlers were women.

In 2021, researchers dated three pieces of wood from the Norse layers that had been cut with metal blades. In 993 a burst of cosmic rays raised the amount of radiocarbon in the air for one year, leaving a marker in that year's tree ring. By finding that ring and counting the rings after it to the bark edge, they showed the trees were felled in 1021.

The 1021 date fixes one year, not the first arrival or the length of stay. Reading the two sagas side by side, the dating team estimates that the Norse came and went over somewhere between about three and thirteen years. Because the sagas were written down centuries later, how closely their details match the site is still argued over. Finds at L'Anse aux Meadows show that it served as a base from which regions further south were explored, but where exactly the Norse went is uncertain. People had lived at the site, on and off, for thousands of years before the Norse came.

L'Anse aux Meadows is the oldest known European site in the Americas, about five hundred years before Columbus. The researchers who fixed the date point out that it also marks the first time humans are known to have circled the globe: the ancestors of Native Americans had crossed from Asia, and now Europeans had reached the same continent from the other direction. The Norse presence itself was brief.

East Polynesia is a scatter of fifteen island groups across the eastern Pacific, including Hawaii, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and Aotearoa (New Zealand). They were the last habitable places on Earth that people reached. The voyagers came from western Polynesia, around Samoa, which had been settled long before. They reached the Society Islands, around Tahiti, in about the 11th century. Between seventy and a few hundred years later they spread in a single burst to almost every remaining island, thousands of kilometres apart, mostly between about 1190 and 1290. The speed of that spread helps explain why people across the region share such closely related languages, cultures and biology.

Two independent lines of evidence now agree on the broad picture. The first is radiocarbon dating. In 2011, Janet Wilmshurst and colleagues reviewed 1,434 radiocarbon dates from across East Polynesia and kept only the most reliable: those from short-lived material, which records a single season of growth rather than the long life of a tree. Those dates put the first arrivals in the Society Islands at about 1025 to 1120, and the spread to the rest of East Polynesia some 70 to 265 years later.

The second is genetics. In 2021, Alexander Ioannidis and colleagues compared the genomes of 430 living people from 21 Pacific island populations. Each new island was founded by a small group from the last one, so some genetic variety was lost at every step. Following that loss, they traced a path from Samoa through Rarotonga in the Cook Islands, to the Society Islands in the 11th century, the Austral Islands and Tuamotus in the 12th, and finally the Marquesas, Raivavae and Rapa Nui, which was reached around 1200 by way of Mangareva. The islands where people raised large stone statues turn out to be closely related.

For decades, many researchers argued that East Polynesia was settled much earlier, with some chronologies differing by more than a thousand years. Wilmshurst and colleagues argue that those older dates came from samples with large built-in errors. Even so, as the 2021 genetic study notes, different archaeological surveys still suggest dates several centuries apart, and the order in which islands were reached was long unknown.

A second question was whether Polynesians and Native Americans ever met. The sweet potato and the bottle gourd, both American plants, were growing in Polynesia before Europeans arrived. In 2020, a genetic study of 807 people from Polynesia and the Pacific coast of the Americas found signs of a single contact around 1200, with a group most closely related to Indigenous people of present-day Colombia. The study placed the contact in eastern Polynesia, before Rapa Nui was settled. Which side made the voyage is not known.

The settlement of East Polynesia completed the human spread across the habitable Earth, apart from Antarctica. It was done by voyaging across an ocean that spans a third of the planet, and it left a family of island societies linked by ancestry and language from Hawaii to Aotearoa.

From the 700s to the 1500s, caravans of hundreds of camels crossed the Sahara. They carried gold, salt, textiles and jewellery between West Africa and the Mediterranean world. Sijilmasa, in what is now Morocco, stood at the northern edge of the desert; Tadmekka and Timbuktu, in today's Mali, stood at the southern edge, linked to the Niger River. West African gold was prized for its purity and was used to mint coins.

In the early 1300s the empire of Mali spread over lands that today lie in Mauritania, Senegal, Mali, Niger and beyond. In 1324 its ruler, Mansa Musa, set out on the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca that Islam asks of every Muslim who is able to make it. On the way he stayed in Cairo, then ruled by the Mamluk sultans. When he returned, he had the Djinguereber mosque built in Timbuktu with the help of scholars and an architect from Andalusia, in Muslim Spain, who came back with him.

Much of what we know about the visit comes from al-Umari, a 14th-century Arab historian who wrote about it at least a decade later. He reports that Musa said he had come for the pilgrimage and nothing else, that he sent loads of unworked gold to the sultan's treasury, and that he gave gold to every emir and officeholder at court. He adds that before the visit a gold coin, the mithqal, was worth at least 25 silver dirhams in Egypt, and that for about twelve years afterwards it was worth no more than 22.

Archaeology fills in the trade itself. Excavations at Sijilmasa, Gao and Tadmekka have found glazed pottery, glass, beads and silk that crossed the desert. Finds in Mali suggest Arabic was spreading south of the Sahara by the 900s. The manuscripts of Timbuktu show scholars there sharing in the learning of the wider Islamic world.

The most famous details are the hardest to check. Modern accounts often repeat that Musa travelled with 8,000 courtiers, 12,000 servants and a hundred camel loads of gold, and he is often called the richest person who ever lived. Numbers like these are repeated widely but are hard to verify, and wealth across seven centuries cannot be compared in any exact way. Al-Umari's report of the gold price is more specific, but it describes one market, in Cairo, over a decade.

West African gold was central to the medieval economy of the Mediterranean world. The trade carried more than gold: Islam, Arabic writing and books crossed the Sahara with the caravans, and Timbuktu drew scholars from across the Islamic world. Medieval West Africa was one of the hubs of the connected Old World.

In 1346 plague broke out in the Golden Horde, the Mongol state on the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas. Over the next seven years it spread around the Black Sea and the Mediterranean and into the lands beyond, reaching Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. The disease is caused by the bacterium *Yersinia pestis*. It survives in populations of wild rodents, from which it can spill over into people. Historians call this outbreak the Black Death, the best-known part of the Second Plague Pandemic.

For a long time the evidence was written, and most of it described parts of western Europe. Genetics has added a new kind of proof: ancient DNA from medieval victims has confirmed that *Yersinia pestis* was the cause.

In 2022, Maria Spyrou and colleagues studied two cemeteries near Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan, where tombstones dated 1338 and 1339 name pestilence as the cause of death. They recovered plague DNA from the buried individuals. The strain turned out to be the common ancestor of a sudden burst of new plague lineages, sometimes called the Big Bang, that is linked with the start of the pandemic. Its closest living relatives are found in rodents of the Tian Shan mountains nearby. The team concluded that the Black Death emerged in this region in the early 1300s.

A different kind of evidence comes from pollen. In 2022, Adam Izdebski and colleagues looked at pollen in 261 dated lake and bog cores from 19 European countries. Fewer people meant fewer fields, so a heavy death toll should show up as a fall in crop pollen and a return of trees and grass.

The usual figure is that the Black Death killed up to half the population of the regions it struck. The pollen study found that some regions did see a sharp collapse in farming, but others carried on almost unchanged. That points to large differences in mortality from place to place, so any single figure for Europe, let alone the whole Old World, is uncertain.

The timing of the origin is also argued. The historian Monica Green argues that the burst of plague lineages began around 1200, and that Mongol armies and trade carried plague across Central Eurasia from the thirteenth century, a hundred years before 1346. In her view there were several separate outbreaks, in China, Central Eurasia and the Black Sea and Mediterranean, rather than one wave moving west. Spyrou and colleagues date the burst to the first half of the fourteenth century instead.

The Black Death has been called the largest pandemic in human history. It also shows how closely the Old World had been tied together by the 1300s: a disease that began among rodents in the mountains of Central Asia reached cities thousands of kilometres away within a few years.
